title: What we look for
desc: Twenty-one kinds in one table, the backwards sensitivity dial, your own kinds of data and the never-hidden list that leaks by design.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can choose categories and a sensitivity level you are able to defend, add an exception without opening a hole, and say what Your own data adds on Enterprise.

steps.title: The shield can be on and still find nothing
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep is a sixty-person installation firm near Zwolle, and its shield is switched on — that was the previous chapter. On its own, that proves nothing. A shield asked the wrong questions reports itself as protecting you while every customer name sails straight past it.

The first two steps on the path set the questions. Open `Settings` → `Organisation` → `Privacy Shield`:

- **1 What we look for** — which kinds of personal data the detector is asked about, and how sure it has to be before a finding counts
- **2 Your own data** — the kinds of data only your organisation has, and the names that are deliberately left visible

Every step saves together, with one button in the bar at the bottom: **Save changes**. The bar names the steps that hold unsaved changes; until you press it, nothing you do here is in force.

steps.title: An unticked kind is never even asked about
steps.bodyMd:
Under **Kinds of personal data** sits one table: **21** kinds, one row each, grouped from Personal and Contact to EU / Netherlands. Labels run from Person Names and Email Addresses to National ID numbers (BSN and equivalents). The column that matters here is **Hide from AI** — its heading counts what you chose, `look for it · 7 of 21` — with `All` and `None` buttons above it. The two columns beside it decide what a tool may carry out; that is the next chapter.

Leave a kind unticked and it is never put to the detector. The question is never asked, so the answer always comes back clean — and nothing in your reports hints at the gap.

Emptying the list is not a choice either. Overview then lists *"No kinds of data are selected"* — "Protection is on, but nothing is ticked — so nothing will ever be found." — while the scanner reads an empty list as "never configured" and scans all 21 anyway. Two parts of the product disagreeing is not a policy: tick what you mean.

steps.title: The dial runs backwards
steps.bodyMd:
**How strict** offers three levels side by side: `Low`, `Balanced` (marked `recommended`) and `High`. Under them the trade-off is written out: *misses more, fewer interruptions* at one end, *hides more, also ordinary words* at the other. Behind them is one number — how sure the detector must be before a finding counts — and it runs opposite to the names: Low sensitivity is **85%**, Balanced **70%**, High sensitivity **45%**. Lower number, more findings.

Balanced is not a split-the-difference compromise. It is the calibrated anchor: every per-category level is tuned and measured at that position, so it is the only setting whose behaviour has actually been tested.

`Advanced: exact percentage` reveals a slider from 10% to 100% in steps of 5, labelled "finds more" at one end and "finds less" at the other. Anything off-preset shows as `Custom · NN%` — a number you will have to justify.

steps.question: Van Dijk Groep's admin opens the advanced slider and sets 90%, reasoning that a higher number must be stricter. What actually happens?

choices.label: Almost nothing is hidden — the detector now has to be 90% sure, and most short messages never score that high.
Everything even slightly personal is hidden, and colleagues start complaining about false alarms.
choices.feedback: That is what a LOW number does. The slider is a confidence threshold, not a strictness score: 10% finds the most, 100% the least.

choices.label: Only the high-risk categories are still checked; names and company names are dropped.
choices.feedback: The threshold never changes which categories are asked — that is the list of categories. It only changes how sure the detector must be about each finding.

choices.label: Nothing changes, because the slider only takes effect once the Balanced card is deselected.
choices.feedback: Moving the slider off a preset value is the deselection — no level stays selected, and a `Custom · 90%` badge appears beside How strict instead.

steps.explanation: The dial is inverted, which is exactly why the three named levels exist. At 85% or above the page pushes back itself, in amber: "At this setting almost nothing is hidden. Short messages usually score between 60% and 85%…". `Balanced` (70%) is the answer you can defend, because that is the level everything was measured at.

steps.title: Your own data: what only you have
steps.bodyMd:
Step 2, **Your own data**, covers what the 21 kinds cannot know about: project code names, contract-number formats, internal system names. It is part of the Enterprise plan; on other plans the step still opens, with the note *"Your own data is part of Enterprise."*, and the **Never hidden** panel beside it works as usual.

Start from an example — *Customer or contract numbers*, *Project code names* — or describe your own and press `Create type`; once you have one, `Add a type` starts the next. A short wizard follows: **Describe**, **Test and tune**, **Where it applies**. Under *How should we recognise it?* you choose `A list of words`, `A fixed format` or `Recognised by AI`. Van Dijk Groep adds one: name `Inkoopcontractnummer`, `A fixed format`, with three real examples such as `VDG-INK-204118`, from which the page proposes the pattern `\bVDG-INK-\d{6}\b`. `Add to the list`, then Save changes.

Each type gets its own placeholder, and is hidden **on top of** whatever the detector finds. A list of words or a fixed format is matched by Bee Flow itself, character for character: no model weighs it up, so the sensitivity setting does not apply and it keeps working when the detection service is down.

steps.title: Never hidden: exact, everywhere, forever
steps.bodyMd:
Beside your own types sits the panel that does the opposite, and it is the one control on these pages that makes the shield leak on purpose. Values under **Never hidden** are left visible to the AI, every time.

Three properties to hold on to:

- **Exact.** Matching is on the normalised value — case, spaces and punctuation ignored — and never a substring. Allowing "Shell" does not allow "Shell Advies BV"; each variant needs its own entry.
- **Everywhere.** **Your own exceptions** apply in **every** category, not just company names.
- **Forever.** There is no expiry. An entry stands until somebody removes it.

Above them, the **Well-known companies** switch is on by default: a list of 221 large companies, brands and public bodies maintained by Bee Flow. That list applies to company names only; yours are not limited that way. The panel's own warning says it plainly: "These reach the AI as written."

steps.question: To keep AI answers readable, the admin adds "Van Dijk" to Your own exceptions under Never hidden. What did they just exempt?

choices.label: Every value that normalises to "vandijk" — in all 21 categories, including a customer or an employee named Van Dijk.
"Van Dijk" and anything containing it, such as "Van Dijk Groep" and "Van Dijk Installatie BV".
choices.feedback: Matching is exact on the normalised value, never a substring — that is deliberate, because substring matching would silently unredact a different company. "Van Dijk Groep" needs its own entry.

choices.label: Only the Company names category, since an allow term is an exception to organisation detection.
choices.feedback: That limit applies to the built-in well-known-companies list. A term you type yourself is honoured whichever detector flagged the value.

choices.label: Nothing yet — your own exceptions only take effect once the Well-known companies switch is turned off.
choices.feedback: The two sources are independent switches. Your own list works whether the built-in list is on or off.

steps.explanation: An allow term is a permanent, cross-category exemption on an exact value. Short and common words are the danger: a surname that doubles as a company name buys you readability in one chat and unredacted people everywhere else. Write the full, specific form — "Van Dijk Groep" — and add each variant you actually need.

steps.title: Four teams, four defensible sets
steps.instruction: The sixty people at Van Dijk Groep sit in four teams, and each works with different data. Match the team to the set of categories that has to be ticked before their work is protected.

pairs.left: Inkoop pastes supplier quotations into chat to compare prices, contract numbers and payment details.
pairs.right: IBAN Numbers, Bank Account Numbers, Tax numbers (VAT / BTW / RSIN)
pairs.note: Financial counterparty data. Company names belongs here too — but tick it and a redacted price comparison becomes unreadable, which is the exact itch that sends admins to the Never hidden list.

pairs.left: HR runs a nightly automation that summarises sick-leave and re-integration files.
pairs.right: National ID numbers (BSN and equivalents), Medical Conditions, Medications
pairs.note: Special-category data plus the BSN. Nobody is watching an automation at night, so the categories are the only protection in the room.

pairs.left: Support pastes a customer e-mail into chat to draft a friendly reply.
pairs.right: Person Names, Email Addresses, Phone Numbers
pairs.note: The everyday case, and the highest volume. If only these three are ticked you already cover most of what leaves a support desk.

pairs.left: IT pastes a server log into chat while debugging a broken connector.
pairs.right: IP Addresses, Passwords and access keys, Web addresses
pairs.note: Logs are personal data too: an IP address identifies a person, and a pasted log is the classic way an access key reaches a model.

steps.title: Read the save bar, not just the button
steps.bodyMd:
The server checks your own types again when you save. If one is refused, the rest of the shield is stored anyway — the save is partial, not refused. So the place you learn a type is not running is the save bar, not just the toast:

- the toast **"Saved successfully!"**, and **"Saved."** in the bar — everything went in
- the toast **"Saved, with notes — see the message below."**, and in the bar "Saved, with notes. 1 of your own types were refused and are not in force. They are marked under Your own data." The row itself reads "Not saved: " and the reason.
- **"Saved, with notes. Your plan does not include: …"** — a setting your plan does not cover was stored at the value it allows

One trap: reloading or closing the page warns you about unsaved changes; clicking to another screen inside the app does not — those edits are gone.

steps.title: Tick your kinds and add one exception — we will verify it
steps.instruction: Open the Privacy Shield. On step 1, What we look for, check the Hide from AI column: tick the kinds of personal data your work really contains, and leave How strict on Balanced unless you can defend another level. Then go to step 2, Your own data, and in the Never hidden panel add your organisation's full name, not the short one. Press Save changes and read the save bar: "Saved." means both are in force. On Enterprise you can also add a type of your own there, but it is not needed for this check. You can remove the exception again afterwards.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Pick categories on purpose.** An unticked kind is never asked about; the Hide from AI column and Overview's **Kinds of data** both count what you chose, and zero is flagged as nothing ever being found.
- **Defend the level, not the word.** Balanced (70%) is the measured setting; a higher percentage finds less, not more, whatever "strict" suggests.
- **Use both lists on Your own data with your eyes open.** Your own types widen the net, and lists of words and fixed formats are matched by Bee Flow itself; Never hidden is exact, applies in every category and never expires — so write the full name, never the short one.

Next chapter: what actually happens to a message once something is found, and what may still leave your organisation.

practiceTopic.title: Privacy Shield detection settings
practiceTopic.summary: How an organisation admin chooses categories, sensitivity and exception lists on the What we look for and Your own data steps.
facts: The Kinds of personal data table holds 21 kinds, one row each, in groups; its Hide from AI column has All and None buttons and a live count in its heading, for example 'look for it · 7 of 21'.
The How strict levels map to confidence thresholds that run backwards: Low sensitivity 85%, Balanced 70% (marked recommended), High sensitivity 45%; lower finds more.
Balanced is the calibrated anchor — every per-category level is tuned and measured at that position — and the advanced slider runs 10% to 100% in steps of 5, from 'finds more' to 'finds less'.

Your own data (Enterprise) adds types through a wizard — Describe, Test and tune, Where it applies — recognised as A list of words, A fixed format or Recognised by AI; types are hidden on top of whatever the detector finds.

Never hidden matches exactly on the normalised value (case, spaces and punctuation ignored); Your own exceptions apply in every category and never expire, while the Well-known companies list of 221 names covers company names only.
Overview shows the row Kinds of data as '{n} of 21' and, at zero, lists 'No kinds of data are selected': 'Protection is on, but nothing is ticked — so nothing will ever be found.'
Saving is one button, Save changes; success toasts 'Saved successfully!', while a refused type still saves everything else and reports 'Saved, with notes' in the save bar.

actionChecks.label: Tick your kinds of data and add an exception
actionChecks.hint: Settings → Organisation → Privacy Shield: tick kinds under Hide from AI on What we look for, add a Never hidden exception on Your own data, then Save changes.

endpoints.returns: the saved shield config object for the learner’s own organisation (membership is enough to read it); piiDetectionCategories[] holds the kinds ticked under Hide from AI on What we look for, and piiAllowTerms[] the Never hidden exceptions as plain strings. Neither field is limited by plan.

criteria.label: At least one kind of data is ticked under Hide from AI
criteria.hint: On What we look for, tick the kinds your work contains in the Hide from AI column and press Save changes.
criteria.rule: GET the org shield config; piiDetectionCategories is a non-empty array (an org that never saved the shield can read a list seeded from the global AI settings)

criteria.label: One exception is saved under Never hidden
criteria.hint: Add your organisation’s full name under Never hidden and press Save changes.
criteria.rule: GET the org shield config; piiAllowTerms is a non-empty array (defaults to [], and the built-in well-known-companies list is a separate flag)
